editorialPolicy.storyFidelity: Each level preserves the complete event sequence, motivations, consequence, and chapter ending.
editorialPolicy.foundation: Concrete 6–11 word sentences, one main action per line, minimal subordinate clauses.
editorialPolicy.core: Connected 10–18 word sentences with cause, contrast, and reaction.
editorialPolicy.studio: Literary but speakable sentences that preserve narrator wit, suspense, and moral tension.
editorialPolicy.safety: Historic slapstick and peril are described without adding graphic detail. Harmful actions retain their consequences and are not presented as desirable.
editorialPolicy.narration: Dialogue is acted with restraint inside one continuous chapter-level performance; no independent sentence generations.

narration.direction: Begin with sincere hopeful plans, let the distant music become increasingly irresistible, and end with a sober reminder of Geppetto shivering at home.
narration.productionRule: Generate one continuous master per level and derive sentence timestamps from that same master.

livingStorybook.artBrief: A wide village-road panorama linking the school path to a colorful but original wooden marionette theater. Pinocchio carries the A-B-C book, musicians and a small crowd draw him sideways, and a ragpicker waits near the ticket entrance while a cold path points back toward Geppetto's home.

lines.text: Pinocchio walked to school with his new book.
He dreamed of helping Geppetto one day.
Then he heard pipes and drums nearby.
The music came from a puppet theater.
A ticket cost four pennies.
Pinocchio had no money for the show.
He sold his A-B-C book to a ragpicker.
At home, Geppetto still shivered without his coat.

lines.text: Pinocchio hurried toward school with the new A-B-C book under his arm.
He imagined learning quickly and buying Geppetto a magnificent coat.
Distant pipes and drums interrupted those generous plans.
He discovered that the music announced a Great Marionette Theater.
Although school waited in the other direction, curiosity pulled him toward the crowd.
The ticket cost four pennies, and Pinocchio did not own even one.
He tried to sell his paper coat, bark shoes, and dough cap.
When nobody wanted them, he finally offered the A-B-C book.
A ragpicker paid four pennies, and Pinocchio entered the theater.
Meanwhile, Geppetto shivered at home after selling his coat for that very book.

lines.text: Pinocchio set out for school rehearsing splendid plans to learn, earn money, and reward Geppetto with a jeweled coat.
His gratitude sounded sincere until the distant rhythm of pipes and drums introduced a more immediate temptation.
At the crossing, school demanded patience in one direction while the marionette theater promised excitement in the other.
Pinocchio postponed responsibility with the convenient belief that tomorrow would always provide enough time for study.
He reached a brilliant wooden theater whose performance was beginning behind a crowd of eager spectators.
The entrance fee was only four pennies, yet it exceeded everything the penniless marionette owned.
His flowered-paper coat, bark shoes, and dough cap proved too useless even for another child to buy.
After hesitation, curiosity defeated gratitude and he offered the A-B-C book purchased through his father's sacrifice.
A ragpicker exchanged four pennies for the book, turning Geppetto's winter coat into a single afternoon of entertainment.
As Pinocchio rushed inside, the narrator leaves us with the image of his father shivering at home in shirt sleeves.
